Issued at 147 AM EDT Mon Sep 14 2026

Incoming high pressure has led to the cessation of the lake effect 
rain showers over the east early this morning and has brought clear 
skies overhead. This, in addition to the antecedent cool air 
overhead, has allowed temperatures to drop down into the mid 30s in 
portions of the interior west as of midnight EDT this morning; 
expect this trend to continue as some spots potentially get into the 
20s. These chilly early Fall low temperatures will create areas of 
frost tonight over the interior west. Thus, a Frost Advisory is in 
effect until 9AM EDT this morning for Gogebic, Ontonagon, southern 
Houghton, Baraga, Iron, and Dickinson counties. While not as 
widespread as the interior west early this morning, some patchy 
frost is also expected in portions of the interior central and east 
too, with some of the more sparsely populated areas of the interior 
east potentially seeing more widespread frost in spots; however, 
given that this area is heavily forested, generally not for ag. use, 
and again sparsely populated, decided to not hoist up a Frost 
Advisory for the southwestern interior portion of Alger County and 
northeastern portion of Delta County. After sunrise this morning 
though, expect the frost threat to dissipate as temperatures warm 
into the 60s by this afternoon. 

Expect a somewhat quiet weather day today, although that changes 
come the mid-to-late afternoon hours as a warm front approaches the 
area. As the warm front approaches, expect winds from the south to 
pick up, with gusts up of 20 to 30 mph being seen over the interior 
areas and downslopes along Lake Superior by the early evening hours. 
In addition, rain showers with potentially a few rumbles of thunder 
thrown in there are expected to begin moving into the western U.P. 
late this afternoon/early this evening. Some of the rainfall could 
be heavy at times, although no flash flooding is expected due to the 
quick-hitting nature of the warm-becoming-occluding front tonight 
and the ongoing drought conditions. The latest HREF shows a general 
25 to 60% chance that over half an inch of rain will fall over most 
of the U.P. between early this evening and Tuesday morning, with a 
near 0% chance around Marquette and a near 100% chance near 
Menominee. While this isn't quite looking to be the wetting rainfall 
that was hoped for yesterday morning, it does seem like it still may 
be able to bring some relief to the drought conditions being seen 
across much of the area. 

While some gusty southerly winds of 25 to 40 mph could be seen 
across the area tonight with the occluding front passing through, 
expect a slight break in the winds before winds pick up from the 
west behind the front on Tuesday as CAA works through the area. 
While wind gusts look to be at about the same speeds or slightly 
weaker across most of the area on Tuesday, westerly wind gusts of 
45+ mph are projected to occur over the Keweenaw during the late 
morning to early afternoon hours. With the LREF even showing a 60-
90% chance of wind gusts over 45 mph by early Tuesday afternoon over 
the Keweenaw, a Wind Advisory may be forthcoming for that portion of 
the Yoop. Some wind gusts around 45 mph or so could also be seen 
along portions of the lakeshore in the west and north central too, 
but given that the stronger winds aren't expected to make it inland, 
no Wind Advisory is expected for these areas as of the current going 
forecast. One more note about the winds: the high winds over the 
Great Lakes tonight through Tuesday is looking to bring dangerous 
swimming conditions back over the Lake Michigan beaches of 
Schoolcraft County through the entire day Tuesday and the Lake 
Superior beaches of Alger County for at least the afternoon hours. 
Therefore, it goes without saying this late in the season that 
swimmers should avoid putting themselves in such a dangerous 
situation and wait for a calmer day to take an early-Fall dip into 
our Great Lakes. As high pressure moves back into the region on 
Tuesday night, expect the winds to rapidly fall off and for the 
skies to become clear, allowing lows to fall into the 30s across 
portions of the interior; some patchy frost may be seen once again 
in the interior west Tuesday night. 

Moving into the rest of the week, expect generally quieter weather 
as zonal flow in the upper levels and shortwave ridges moving 
through the U.P. generally keep active weather away. While this 
should keep temperatures fairly seasonable for the rest of the week, 
this does also support dry weather continuing until the end of the 
forecast period, provided we don't get grazed by a nearby shortwave.
